column3: Auwers, A. (1891) Der Sonnendurchmesser und der Venusdurchmesser nach den Beobachtungen an den Heliometern der deutschen Venus-Expeditionen. Astronomische Nachrichten 128, 361
column5: Origin of 959.63 arcseconds at 1 au. Not read; cited through McGlaun, Quaglia et al. 2021 and Wright and Young 2024.

column3: McGlaun, D. Arthur Auwers and the Solar Radius (solareclipses.com)
column5: Account of Auwers' data sources, weighting method and adoption by the IAU; read via WebFetch summary. Author is the developer of the solareclipses.com eclipse software.

column3: Meeus, J. (1991) Astronomical Algorithms, chapter Semidiameters of the Sun, Moon, and Planets
column5: Gives the Sun's semidiameter at unit distance as 959.63 arcseconds. Read from a local OCR copy of the first edition (var/downloads/meeus_aa_1991.txt).

column3: Rozelot, J.-P. and Kosovichev, A. (2026) Sharper Than Ever: Do Modern Observations Pin Down the Solar Radius to Converge on New Standards? arXiv:2605.23794
column5: Review tabulating canonical, seismic, photospheric, eclipse and nominal radii with km and arcsecond values and a proposed glossary. Full PDF read. Contains a typo giving the canonical value as 965.63.

column3: Rozelot, J.-P., Kosovichev, A. G. and Kilcik, A. (2016) A brief history of the solar diameter measurements: a critical quality assessment of the existing data. arXiv:1609.02710
column5: History of ground, eclipse and space measurements; source for the Emilio 2015 HMI and AIA values and for the 0.41 arcsecond, 297 km gap between Auwers and the nominal radius. Full PDF read.

column3: Prša, A. et al. (2016) Nominal values for selected solar and planetary quantities: IAU 2015 Resolution B3. AJ 152, 41
column5: Defines the nominal solar radius 6.957e8 m and explains that it is the rounded Haberreiter et al. value 695,658 ± 140 km at Rosseland optical depth 2/3. Full arXiv PDF read.

column3: Haberreiter, M., Schmutz, W. and Kosovichev, A. G. (2008) Solving the discrepancy between the seismic and photospheric solar radius. ApJ 675, L53
column5: Inflection point lies 0.347 ± 0.006 Mm above tau5000 = 1 and 0.333 ± 0.008 Mm above tauRoss = 2/3; photospheric radius 695.66 Mm. Abstract read on arXiv and Semantic Scholar.

column3: Schou, J., Kosovichev, A. G., Goode, P. R. and Dziembowski, W. A. (1997) Determination of the Sun's seismic radius from the SOHO Michelson Doppler Imager. ApJ 489, L197
column5: Seismic radius 695,680 ± 30 km from f modes l = 88 to 250. Not read; value taken from Rozelot and Kosovichev 2026.

column3: Brown, T. M. and Christensen-Dalsgaard, J. (1998) Accurate determination of the solar photospheric radius. ApJ 500, L195
column5: Solar Diameter Monitor 1981 to 1987 at 800 nm: 695.508 ± 0.026 Mm. Abstract read via Semantic Scholar.

column3: Kosovichev, A. G. and Rozelot, J.-P. (2018) Cyclic changes of the Sun's seismic radius. ApJ 861, 90
column5: Seismic radius reduced by 1 to 2 km at solar maxima; 5 to 8 km at 5 Mm depth. Abstract read via Semantic Scholar.

column3: Emilio, M., Kuhn, J. R., Bush, R. I. and Scholl, I. F. (2012) Measuring the solar radius from space during the 2003 and 2006 Mercury transits. ApJ 750, 135
column5: SOHO/MDI: 960.12 ± 0.09 arcseconds (696,342 ± 65 km). Abstract read on arXiv.

column3: Emilio, M., Couvidat, S., Bush, R. I., Krucker, S. and Kuhn, J. R. (2015) Measuring the solar radius from space during the 2012 Venus transit. ApJ 798, 48
column5: SDO/HMI 617.3 nm: 959.57 ± 0.02 arcseconds (695,946 ± 15 km); AIA 963.04 at 160 nm and 961.76 at 170 nm. Not read directly; values from Rozelot et al. 2016 and Meftah et al. 2018.

column3: Meftah, M. et al. (2014) Ground-based measurements of the solar diameter during the rising phase of solar cycle 24. A&A 569, A60
column5: SODISM II at Calern, 2011 to 2013, 535.7 nm: 959.78 ± 0.19 arcseconds (696,113 ± 138 km). Abstract read via Semantic Scholar.

column3: Meftah, M. et al. (2018) Solar radius determined from PICARD/SODISM observations and extremely weak wavelength dependence in the visible and the near-infrared. A&A 616, A64
column5: Inflection-point radius 696,134 ± 261 km at 535.7 nm, 696,156 ± 145 km at 607.1 nm, 696,192 ± 247 km at 782.2 nm; about 330 km between seismic and photospheric definitions. Abstract read via Semantic Scholar; the A&A site refused fetches.

column3: Lamy, P., Prado, J.-Y., Floyd, O., Rocher, P., Faury, G. and Koutchmy, S. (2015) A novel technique for measuring the solar radius from eclipse light curves: results for 2010, 2012, 2013, and 2015. Solar Physics 290, 2617
column5: Seventeen photometer light curves at 540 nm with Kaguya limb profiles: 959.99 ± 0.06 arcseconds (696,246 ± 45 km). Abstract read on the Springer page; full text paywalled.

column3: Kilcik, A., Sigismondi, C., Rozelot, J. P. and Guhl, K. (2009) Solar radius determination from total solar eclipse observations on 29 March 2006. Solar Physics 257, 237
column5: Reports 959.22 ± 0.04 arcseconds from Turkey and Egypt observations; abstract read on the Springer page. The method is image based and differs from bead timing.

column3: Quaglia, L., Irwin, J., Emmanouilidis, K. and Pessi, A. (2021) Estimation of the eclipse solar radius by flash spectrum video analysis. ApJS 256, 36
column5: Defines the eclipse solar radius, reports 959.95 ± 0.05 arcseconds from the 2017 flash spectrum at the southern limit, gives duration and limit-distance sensitivity to the radius and compares Occult, Solar Eclipse Maestro and Irwin's model. Full arXiv PDF read.

column3: Raponi, A. and Sigismondi, C. (2011) Solar limb darkening function from Baily's beads observations. arXiv:1112.0403, Il Nuovo Cimento
column5: Photospheric light detected at least 0.65 arcseconds beyond the inflection point; Occult 4 simulates with 959.63 arcseconds; bead corrections depend on equipment. Full PDF read.

column3: Sigismondi, C. (2012) Solar diameter, eclipses and transits: the importance of ground-based observations. arXiv:1211.4394, Mem. S.A.It.
column5: Describes the IOTA bead reduction against 959.63 arcseconds, the 0.7 arcsecond emission blend above the photosphere, the 0.3 to 0.5 arcsecond per second limb speed and the Watts versus Kaguya accuracy. Full PDF read.

column3: Adassuriya, J. et al. (2011) Solar radius determination using Baily beads observations of annular solar eclipse of 15 January 2010. Proceedings of the Technical Sessions, Institute of Physics Sri Lanka 27, 107
column5: Eight beads at the southern limit, Occult 4.0.8.6 with DE423 and Kaguya: 959.89 ± 0.18 arcseconds. Conference proceedings; full PDF read.

column3: Fiala, A. D., Dunham, D. W. and Sofia, S. (1994) Variation of the solar diameter from solar eclipse observations, 1715-1991. Solar Physics 152, 97
column5: Programme to reduce all eclipse edge observations since 1715 with consistent ephemerides. Abstract read on the Springer page; no radius value in the abstract.

column3: Dunham, D. W., Sofia, S., Fiala, A. D., Herald, D. and Muller, P. M. (1980) Observations of a probable change in the solar radius between 1715 and 1979. Science 210, 1243
column5: Bead timings at both path edges in 1715, 1976 and 1979 gave a contraction of 0.34 ± 0.2 arcseconds in 264 years. Not read; figure from a search-engine summary of the abstract.

column3: Kubo, Y. (1993) Position and radius of the Sun determined by solar eclipses in combination with lunar occultations. PASJ 45, 819
column5: Flash-spectrum photometry at the 1970, 1973, 1980 and 1991 eclipses with Watts profiles gave 959.74 to 959.88 arcseconds. Not read; range quoted from Quaglia et al. 2021.

column3: Dunham, D. W., Sofia, S., Guhl, K. and Herald, D. (2016) IOTA solar radius results from eclipses since the 1990s, in Solar and Stellar Flares and their Effects on Planets (IAU proceedings)
column5: IOTA range printed by Quaglia et al. as 956.40 to 956.80 arcseconds, evidently 959.40 to 959.80. Not read; cited through Quaglia et al. 2021 and Rozelot et al. 2016.

column3: Dunham, D. (2024) April 8th total solar eclipse, the ultimate lunar occultation, updated 2024 May 6 (IOTA)
column5: IOTA's 2024 campaign page: Jubier's map uses the 1976 radius, Irwin's 959.95 ± 0.05 limit, the 0.7 km and 10 s corrections, the 2 km umbral-depth rule, and IOTA's retraction of radius variation. Read via curl on 2026-09-15.

column3: Wright, E. and Young, C. A. (2024) A raster-oriented method for creating eclipse maps. AJ 168, 163
column5: Section 6.4 gives NASA's position: figures assume 696,000 km, nominal 695,700 km is unsuitable, eclipse values 959.99, 959.95, 959.98, 960.01 listed, Irwin's map shifted the northern limit several city blocks, 1 s of duration near a limit equals 0.03 arcseconds. Read from a saved copy of the IOP HTML (var/downloads/iop_ad6b23_wayback.html).

column3: NASA SVS 4515 (2016) 2017 Path of Totality, visualizations by Ernie Wright
column5: Constants block: Earth 6378.137 km, Moon 1737.4 km, Sun 696,000 km (959.645 arcsec at 1 AU), DE421, ΔT 68.917 s. svs.gsfc.nasa.gov was unreachable; read from a web.archive.org snapshot dated 2018 fetched 2026-09-15.

column3: NASA SVS 5073 (2023) The 2023 and 2024 Solar Eclipses: Map and Data
column5: Lists SRTM, LRO LOLA, SLDEM2015 and DE421 as inputs; no solar radius printed. Read from a locally saved copy and a web.archive.org snapshot of 2024 fetched 2026-09-15.

column3: NASA SVS 5365 (2024) Broken Annular Baily's Beads Simulation, visualizations by Ernie Wright
column5: Links the 2024 AJ paper as the method behind the 2024 maps; no radius printed. Read from a web.archive.org snapshot of 2024 fetched 2026-09-15.

column3: Besselian Elements team (Quaglia, Irwin). Measuring the Solar Radius during Total Solar Eclipses
column5: States the eclipse solar radius 959.95 ± 0.05 arcseconds and the flash-spectrum method. Read via curl on 2026-09-15.

column3: Besselian Elements team. The solar radius and its impact on eclipse computations
column5: 2017 Vale example: centreline 130 s to 128 s, southern edge 34 s to 13 s for 959.63 versus about 960 arcseconds; notes Solar Eclipse Maestro allows changing the radius. Read via curl on 2026-09-15.

column3: McGlaun, D. Calculating Besselian Elements (solareclipses.com)
column5: Gives 959.95 arcseconds as 696,221.3 km and k = 0.272399309 from the 1737.4 km LRO datum. Read via WebFetch summary.

column3: Jubier, X. Solar Eclipse Google Map Help
column5: States the maps use the IAU 1976 radius 959.63 arcseconds and that the true photospheric radius is closer to 959.98 ± 0.02 arcseconds. Read via curl on 2026-09-15.

column3: Espenak, F. Solar Eclipse Predictions and the Mean Lunar Radius (EclipseWise)
column5: k = 0.2725076 for penumbral contacts and 0.272281 for umbral contacts, with the USNO 1968 to 1980 history. Read via WebFetch; contains no solar radius statement.

column3: Espenak, F. Explanation of Solar Eclipse Predictions (NASA GSFC)
column5: DE200/LE200 ephemerides, smaller k for umbral contacts, no limb corrections in the base predictions, graze-zone definition. Read via curl on 2026-09-15.

column3: US Naval Observatory. Solar Eclipse Computer
column5: States Sun 696,000 km and Moon 1737.4 km as IAU-adopted values; no limb profiles or centre-of-figure corrections. Read via WebFetch.

column3: US Naval Observatory. 2024 April 8 Total Solar Eclipse
column5: Repeats the 696,000 km and 1737.4 km constants for the 2024 predictions. Read via WebFetch.

column5: Uses 696,000 km with a comment that NASA's predictions use 696,000 km from the arctangent of 959.63 arcseconds, and k = 0.2725076 for both cones. Read from a local copy of the file.

column5: [sun] radius=696000., [moon] radius=1737.4, [earth] radius=6378.1366. Read via WebFetch of the raw file.

column5: Lunar eclipses only; uses a solar radius of 696,340 km and a lunar radius of 1737.1 km without a cited source. Read via WebFetch of the raw file.

column5: Bead simulator defaults to 959.95 arcseconds (Quaglia et al. 2021), user adjustable, not used for contact times; smooth-Moon contact times; Kaguya/Herald limb with 1,800 points at 0.2 degrees. Read via WebFetch.

column5: Shaded areas may be off by a few hundred metres; advises moving a few hundred metres toward the centre. Read via curl on 2026-09-15; the 2D map help page returned 403.

column5: Describes Irwin's 959.95 arcsecond map, the narrower northern edge and the Texas southern-edge anomaly, with comments from C. Alex Young. Read via curl on 2026-09-15.
